We discuss some consequences of the spectral theorem and of our study of unitary and orthogonal matrices that are important in applications.


## The LU decomposition

This decomposition actually has nothing to do with the spectral theorem; it's just a restatement of Gaussian elimination, but it will be useful to have for reference at this point.

**Proposition:** Let $A$ be an $n\times m$ matrix (over any field).  Then there exist an $n\times n$ permutation matrix $P$, an $n\times n$ matrix $L$, and an $n\times m$ matrix $U$, where $L$ is lower triangular and $U$ is upper triangular ($u_{ij}=0$ when $i>j$), such that $PA=LU$.

The proof is just Gaussian elimination. 
Start with $A$ and apply row operations to it so that it becomes upper triangular.  Generically, each diagonal entry in turn can serve as a pivot, and the row operations correspond to left multiplication of $A$ by a sequence $E_1,\ldots,E_k$ of elementary matrices that are lower triangular with ones on the diagonal. 
So
$$
E_{k}E_{k-1}\cdots E_{1}A = U
$$
and then $L=(E_{k}E_{k-1}\cdots E_{1})^{-1}$. 

In the general case one may need to permute the rows of $A$ so that a nonzero pivot is available at each step.  Then one collects those permutations into a permutation matrix $P$ and replaces $A$ by $PA$.  If $A$ is singular (or not square), $U$ may have zeros on its diagonal.  We won't treat any of these special cases in detail here. 

## The QR decomposition

Let $X$ be an $n\times k$ matrix with real or complex entries.  The $QR$ decomposition says that (assuming the columns of $X$ are linearly independent) we can find an $n\times n$ orthogonal (or unitary) matrix $Q$ and an $n\times k$ upper triangular matrix $R$ such that
$$
X = QR.
$$

This is just a version of the Gram--Schmidt algorithm.  Gram--Schmidt applied to the columns $x_1,\ldots, x_k$ of $X$ yields an orthonormal sequence of vectors
$u_1,\ldots, u_k$ where (setting $U$ to the matrix with columns equal to the $u_{i}$):
$$
U = XS
$$

where $S$ is $k\times k$ and upper triangular.  (See the [Gram--Schmidt process](../Week5-6/W05.1.qmd#gram-schmidt)). Then 
$X=US^{-1}$. Extend $U$ by adding orthonormal columns to make it an orthogonal/unitary $n\times n$ matrix $Q$ and add zero rows to
$S^{-1}$ so that it becomes an upper triangular $n\times k$ matrix; this extended matrix is the matrix $R$. This gives us $X=QR$ as claimed.


### Application to Least Squares

Recall our discussion of the least squares problem.  We are given an $N\times k$ matrix $X$.  Each row represents a set of measurements, or features, of a piece of sample data, and the $N$ rows together represent a full set of measurements.  We also have, for each sample, a dependent, target variable whose values
form an $N\times 1$ vector $Y$. We believe there are "weights" $m_{j}$ such that
$$
y_{i} = \sum_{j=1}^{k} m_{j}x_{ij}+b + \epsilon_i
$$
where $\epsilon_i$ is a random error.  

We let $M$ be the $(k+1)\times 1$ vector whose entries are the $m_{j}$ and set $m_{k+1}=b$.  We also let $X'$
be the matrix obtained from $X$ by adding a column of $1$'s.  Then (thinking of $\epsilon$ as a random vector) the equation above becomes
$$
Y = X'M + \epsilon
$$

We showed that the "best" choice for the $m_{j}$ and $b$, in the sense that it minimizes the squared error
$$
S(M) = \|Y-X'M\|^2
$$

is given by solving the "normal equations"
$$
(X')^{\top}Y = (X')^{\top}X'M
$$

Use Gram--Schmidt, as in the QR decomposition, to write $X'=US^{-1}=UK$ where $U$ has orthonormal columns and $K$ is a $(k+1)\times (k+1)$ upper triangular matrix. Then:
$$
(X')^{\top} = K^{\top}U^{\top}
$$
and
$$
(X')^{\top}X' = K^{\top}U^{\top}UK
$$

Since $U$ has orthonormal columns, $U^{\top}U$ is the
$(k+1)\times (k+1)$ identity matrix.  Also (assuming the columns of $X'$ were linearly independent) the matrix $K$ is invertible so the "normal equations" 
become

$$
U^{\top}Y = KM
$$

Since $K$ is upper triangular, you can solve this system by "back substitution".

### The QR decomposition and finding eigenvalues

The QR decomposition is the basis for a standard numerical algorithm for the computation of the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix.  While it can be applied to general matrices (with some caveats) we will consider positive real symmetric matrices for simplicity. 

#### Motivation

Suppose $A$ is a positive real $n\times n$ symmetric matrix with eigenvalues
$\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}>\cdots>\lambda_{n}$.   We know that there exists an orthonormal basis $u_1,\ldots, u_{n}$ of corresponding eigenvectors for $A$.

Choose a vector $v=v_{0}$ at random and consider the following iteration:

- Set $v_{k+1}=Av_{k}/\|Av_{k}\|$

Then the sequence $v_{k}$ converges to the eigenvector $u_{1}$ corresponding to
the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{1}$.

To see why this works, write
$$
v_{0} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} u_{i}
$$
where $\sum |a_{i}|^2 =1$ and $\langle v_{0},u_{1}\rangle = a_{1}$.  We assume $a_{1}\not=0$, which holds with probability one for a randomly chosen $v_{0}$.

Now $v_{k}$ is a unit vector that points in the direction of $A^{k}v_{0}$.
But
$$\begin{aligned}
A^{k}v_{0} &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}\lambda_{i}^{k}u_{i} \\
&= \lambda_{1}^{k} \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}(\lambda_{i}^{k}/\lambda_{1}^{k}) u_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$
Since $\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{i}$ for $i>1$, we see that 
$$
A^{k}v_{0} = \lambda_{1}^{k}(a_{1}u_{1}+e)
$$
where $e\to 0$ at least as fast as $(\lambda_{2}/\lambda_{1})^k$.  The normalized
vector $v_{k}$ therefore gradually aligns with $u_{1}$ as $k\to\infty$. 

 ### The full algorithm

Conceptually, the full QR algorithm uses the same idea we just discussed, but
 at each stage we don't just normalize $Av_{k}$, but we successively apply Gram--Schmidt
 to $A^{k}$, so each column converges to the corresponding element $u_{i}$ of an orthonormal basis. 




**Algorithm:** Let $A=A_0$ be an $n\times n$ real symmetric matrix.  Define 
a sequence of matrices:

- Let $A_{k} = Q_{k} R_{k}$ be the $QR$ decomposition of $A_{k}$.
- Let $A_{k+1}=R_{k}Q_{k}$.  

Notice that $A_{k+1}=Q_{k}^{-1}A_{k}Q_{k}$ so all matrices $A_{j}$ are orthogonally equivalent and have the same eigenvalues.

In addition if we put 
$$
\overline{Q}_{k}=Q_{0}Q_{1}\cdots Q_{k-1}
$$
and
$$
\overline{R}_{k} =R_{k-1}R_{k-2}\cdots R_{0}
$$
then
$$A_{k} = \overline{Q}_{k}^{\top}A\overline{Q}_{k}
$$
and
$$
A^{k} = \overline{Q}_{k}\overline{R}_{k}.
$$

We can compute $\overline{Q}_{k}$ directly by applying Gram--Schmidt to the columns of $A^{k}$. 

The sequence $A_{j}$ converges to a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues of $A$. The sequence $\overline{Q}_{k}$ converges to a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $A$. 

Let
$$
A= \begin{pmatrix}
2.1948 &  0.5638 \\
0.5638 &  2.6052 \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

The algorithm above generates a sequence of (symmetric) matrices $A_{k}$, all similar to $A$ which converge to a diagonal matrix, thereby revealing the eigenvalues of $A$.

The animation below plots the level curves $u^{\top}A_{k}u=1$ where $u=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}$.  These are ellipses, each obtained from the previous one by a rotation by an orthogonal matrix. Ultimately the major and minor axes lie along the $x$ and $y$ axes, which is what happens when $A_{k}$ approaches its limiting diagonal form.

The second graph shows the decay in the off-diagonal entry in the matrix $A_{k}$. It decays linearly with $\log(\lambda_{2}/\lambda_{1})$ where $\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}$ are the eigenvalues of $A$.

{{< embed QR-algorithm-animation.ipynb#qr-animation >}}

We will not pursue a full exploration of the convergence of the QR algorithm, but we will sketch why it works in
the simple case of a positive definite symmetric matrix with distinct eigenvalues.

**Proposition:** Let $A$ be a positive definite real symmetric $n\times n$ matrix, with eigenvalues $\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}>\cdots>\lambda_{n}>0$. Then the sequence $A_{k}$ of matrices introduced above converges to a diagonal matrix $\Lambda$ with entries $\{\lambda_{j}\}$.  The rate of convergence is of order $\rho^{k}$ where $\rho=\max_{j}\frac{\lambda_{j+1}}{\lambda_{j}}$.

To see where this comes from, remember that $A$ is orthogonally similar to a diagonal matrix, so there is 
an orthogonal matrix $V$ such that $A=V\Lambda V^{\top}=V\Lambda V^{-1}$.
Then $A^{k}=V\Lambda^{k}V^{-1}$.  Write $V^{-1}=LU$ using the LU decomposition, where $L$ is lower triangular with ones on the diagonal.  (We assume, as is true generically, that no row permutation is needed.)  Then
$$
A^{k} = V\Lambda^{k}LU=V(\Lambda^{k}L\Lambda^{-k})\Lambda^{k}U
$$

The sequence of matrices $\Lambda^{k}L\Lambda^{-k}$ 
converges to the identity, because its $(i,j)$ entry is $\ell_{ij}(\lambda_{i}/\lambda_{j})^{k}$, and for entries below the diagonal ($i>j$) the ratio $\lambda_{i}/\lambda_{j}$ is less than $1$.  In other words, 
$$
\Lambda^{k}L\Lambda^{-k}=I+E_{k}
$$
where $E_{k}$ is a matrix whose entries are $O(\rho^{k})$. 

If we look at the $QR$ decomposition of 
$$
I+E_{k}=\tilde{Q}_{k}\tilde{R}_{k}
$$
we can see that the two matrices on the right converge to the identity.  This is because the $QR$ decomposition varies continuously (Gram--Schmidt is continuous in its inputs), and the $QR$ decomposition of $I$ is $Q=I$ and $R=I$. 

Now write
$$
A^{k} = V\tilde{Q}_{k}\tilde{R}_{k}\Lambda^{k}U
$$
The first term is orthogonal, and the second upper triangular.
So this is a $QR$ decomposition of $A^{k}$. 

The only ambiguity in the Gram--Schmidt process comes from "reversing the direction" of the unit vectors in each column.  As a result, if $A^{k}=\overline{Q}_{k}\overline{R}_{k}$ and also $A^{k}=QR$ for some other $Q$ and $R$, then $Q=\overline{Q}_{k}D$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix with entries $\pm 1$. In our case this means that
$$
V\tilde{Q}_{k}D_{k} = \overline{Q}_{k}
$$

Now 
$$\begin{aligned}
A_{k} = \overline{Q}_{k}^{\top}A\overline{Q}_{k} &= D_{k}\tilde{Q}_{k}^{\top}(V^{\top}AV)\tilde{Q}_{k}D_{k}\\
&= D_{k}\tilde{Q}_{k}^{\top}\Lambda\tilde{Q}_{k}D_{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\tilde{Q}_{k}\to I$ and $D_{k}\Lambda D_{k}=\Lambda$, we see that $A_{k}\to \Lambda$.



## The Polar Decomposition

The polar decomposition is, in some sense, a generalization of the "polar form" of a complex number, where $z\not=0$ can be written $z=re^{i\theta}$ with $r>0$ and $\theta$ determined up to a multiple of $2\pi$. 

Recall that a self-adjoint linear operator $L$ on an inner product space $V$ is *positive* if $\langle Lv,v\rangle\ge 0$ for all $v\in V$.

Suppose that $L$ is a positive self-adjoint linear operator on an $n$-dimensional (real or complex) inner product space $V$.

Under these hypotheses, $L$ is unitarily (or orthogonally) diagonalizable with nonnegative real eigenvalues $\{\lambda_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}$ and has a spectral resolution

$$
L = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_{i}p_{i}
$$

where $p_{i}$ is the orthogonal projection onto the $\lambda_{i}$-eigenspace of $L$.

**Definition:** The square root $B=\sqrt{L}$ of $L$ is the operator
$$
B = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}p_{i}
$$

(taking the nonnegative square roots).

Using the properties of the $p_{i}$ one checks immediately
that $B^{2}=L$. The map $B$ is positive, self-adjoint, and is the unique positive operator whose square is $L$. 


Now suppose $A$ is any linear operator $A:V\to V$.  Then $A^{*}A:V\to V$ is self-adjoint and positive since
$$
\langle A^{*}Av,v\rangle = \langle Av, Av\rangle = \|Av\|^2\ge 0.
$$

Conversely if $L$ is positive and $A=\sqrt{L}$ then 
$L=A^{*}A$. 

**Proposition:** $L$ is positive if and only if $L=A^{*}A$ for some operator $A$.

For example, the matrix $D=X^{\top}X$ that came up in the equations for least squares regression is positive.

Now suppose that $L$ is any linear operator $L:V\to V$ where $V$ is a real or complex (finite-dimensional) inner product space. 
We will establish the following proposition.

**Proposition (The Polar Decomposition):** Let $L:V\to V$ be a linear operator on a real or complex inner product space.  Then there exist a positive operator $P$ and a unitary (or orthogonal) operator $U$ such that $L=UP$.
Here $P$ is unique and, if $L$ is invertible, $U$ is unique. 

Alternatively, there is a positive operator $P'$ and a unitary (or orthogonal) operator $U'$ such that $L=P'U'$ where $P'$ is unique and $U'$ is unique if $L$ is invertible. 

To construct $U$ and $P$ from $L$, notice first that if $P$ and $U$ exist, then because
$L^{*}L=P^{*}U^{*}UP=P^2$ we must have $P=\sqrt{L^{*}L}$ by the uniqueness of positive square roots.  From the equation
$$
L(v)=UP(v)
$$

we see that if $w\in\image(P)$, say $w=Pv$, then we can define a map $U$ by setting $U(w)=L(v)$.  

This is well-defined.  To see this, observe that 
$$
\|P(v)\|^2=\langle P(v),P(v)\rangle = \langle P^2(v),v\rangle = \langle L^{*}L(v),v\rangle = \|L(v)\|^2.
$$

Thus if $w=Pv_1=Pv_2$, then $P(v_1-v_2)=0$, so $L(v_1-v_2)=0$ by the norm identity we just proved. 

Note further that 
if $w,w'\in\image(P)$, so $w=Pv$ and $w'=Pv'$, 
then $U(aw+w')=aL(v)+L(v')=aU(w)+U(w')$ so $U$ is linear. 

Now, if $w=Pv$ then $\|Uw\|^2=\|UPv\|^2=\|L(v)\|^2=\|P(v)\|^2=\|w\|^2$
so $U$ is an isometry on the image of $P$.  

From the construction above, we see that $U$ is an isometry from the image of $P$ onto the image of $L$. Therefore these
two spaces have the same dimension. 
Choose an orthonormal basis for $\image(P)$, say $u_1,\ldots, u_h$.  The value of $U$ is determined on these $u_{i}$ and
$U(u_1),\ldots, U(u_{h})$ is a basis for $\image(L)$.  Extend the basis $\{u_{i}\}$ of $\image(P)$ to an orthonormal basis of
$V$ by adding $u_{h+1},\ldots, u_{n}$. Then choose an orthonormal basis $w_{h+1},\ldots, w_{n}$ for $\image(L)^{\perp}$.
We can define $U$ on all of $V$ by the definition above on $\image(P)$ and then $U(u_{j})=w_{j}$ for $j=h+1,\ldots, n$.
This gives us an isometry (equivalently a unitary/orthogonal operator) on all of $V$ that satisfies $L=UP$.

In the special case where $L$ is invertible, $P$ must also be invertible and then $U$ is determined ($U=LP^{-1}$) so $P$ and $U$ are unique in this case.

A similar construction handles the decomposition $L=P'U'$. 

**Proposition:** Over the complex numbers, a unitary operator $U$ has the form $\exp(iJ)$ where $J$ is a self-adjoint operator.

**Proof:** $U$ is unitarily diagonalizable and its eigenvalues are all complex numbers of absolute value 1, hence of the 
form $\exp(i\theta)$ for real $\theta$.  So let $J$ be the operator that acts by $\theta$ on the eigenspace where $U$
acts by $\exp(i\theta)$.  Then $U=\exp(iJ)$ and since $J$ is unitarily diagonalizable with real eigenvalues it is self-adjoint.

## The Singular Value Decomposition

The Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) is a version of the spectral theorem that applies to non-square matrices.
Let $X$ be a real $n\times m$ matrix and let $D=X^{\top}X$.  $D$ is apositive symmetric $m\times m$ matrix and so we can apply
the spectral theorem to find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $P^{\top}DP=\Lambda$ where $\Lambda$ is diagonal.
Put another way:
$$
DP = P\Lambda
$$

which expresses the fact that the columns of $P$ are orthonormal eigenvectors for $D$.

Let's set $A=XP$.  Then $A^{\top}A=P^{\top}X^{\top}XP=\Lambda$.   This means that the columns of $A$ are orthogonal but not necessarily orthonormal. 

From a geometric point of view, the entries of each row of $A$ are the coordinates of the corresponding row of $X$ in the orthonormal basis given by the columns of $P$. 

If $D$ is positive definite, so all the $\lambda_{i}>0$, then we can normalize the columns of $A$ by setting $A_{1}=A\Lambda^{-1/2}$.  This happens if and only if $X$ has rank $m\le n$. 
In this case $A_{1}^{\top}A_{1}=\Lambda^{-1/2}\Lambda\Lambda^{-1/2}=I$.
So $A_{1}$ has orthonormal columns. 

If $D$ has zero eigenvalues, then the matrix $A$ will have zero columns corresponding to the zero eigenvalues. So let's order the eigenvalues in descending order of size and suppose $\lambda_{r+1},\ldots, \lambda_{m}$ are all zero.  In this case, the rank of $X$ is $r$. Drop columns $r+1,\ldots, m$ from $A$, yielding $A_{r}$, and "shrink" $\Lambda$ so that it is $r\times r$
with the nonzero eigenvalues on the diagonal, yielding $\Lambda_{r}$.  Let $A_{1}=A_{r}\Lambda_{r}^{-1/2}$ as before. This $A_{1}$ is $n\times r$ and has orthonormal
columns. 

Complete the columns of $A_{1}$ to obtain an orthogonal $n\times n$ matrix $U$ by adding orthonormal columns $u_{r+1},\ldots, u_{n}$.
Let $\sigma_{i}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}$ for $i=1,\ldots,m$ and let $\Sigma$ be the $n\times m$ "diagonal" matrix constructed from these "singular values."

The key point now is that, in the product $U\Sigma$, the first $r$ columns are multiplied by the nonzero $\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}$, so 
the first $r$ columns of $U\Sigma$ give the matrix $A_{1}\Lambda_{r}^{1/2}$, which agrees with the first $r$ columns of $A=XP$. 
The remaining columns of $U\Sigma$ are zero, which agrees with the remaining columns of $A=XP$.  

Therefore:
$$
XP = U\Sigma
$$

or $X=U\Sigma P^{\top}$ where $U$ is orthogonal, $\Sigma$ is $n\times m$ "diagonal", and $P$ is orthogonal. This is called the *singular value decomposition* of $X$.  The diagonal entries of $\Sigma$ are called the singular values and are uniquely determined. 

The "reduced" form of this decomposition keeps only the first $r$ columns of $U$, leaving an $n\times r$ matrix $U_{r}$; the first $r$ diagonal entries of $\Sigma$, leaving an $r\times r$ diagonal matrix $\Sigma_{r}$; and the first $r$ columns of $P$, yielding an $m\times r$ matrix $P_{r}$.   Then
$$
X = U_{r}\Sigma_{r}P_{r}^{\top}.
$$
